avoid_with.name: Eucalyptus

avoid_with.name: Vinegar

avoid_with.name: Birch tar oil + Coffee + Clove Bud

avoid_with.name: Isovaleric acid
avoid_with.reason: can make animalic realism feel oddly polished

Benz Sal.mixing_notes_full:
Benzyl salicylate is one of the industry's classic blending materials rather than a note that is intended to stand out on its own. Most perfumers describe it as a modifier, fixative, and bridge between floral, woody, and balsamic materials. Its odor is relatively mild—a soft sweet floral with powdery, balsamic, slightly solar and faintly marine facets—so its value lies less in contributing a recognizable smell and more in making other ingredients feel smoother, rounder, and more natural. Because of its high molecular weight and low volatility, it also slows the evaporation of more volatile floral materials, making fragrances feel richer and longer-lasting. ScenTree specifically notes its widespread use in white floral compositions, its slight marine/iodized nuance, and its role in stabilizing fragrances and even sunscreen products because it also functions as a UV absorber.

Professionally, benzyl salicylate is most commonly paired with jasmine, ylang-ylang, tuberose, lily-of-the-valley, orange blossom, heliotrope, hydroxycitronellal, coumarin, woody materials, patchouli, and soft musks. One of the most famous historical accords is the eugenol (clove)–benzyl salicylate accord, sometimes called the Mellis accord, which formed the backbone of many classic oriental fragrances including Youth Dew, Opium, Coco, Tabu, and L'Air du Temps. Rather than smelling obviously of clove or salicylate, the combination produces a rich spicy-floral warmth that became characteristic of twentieth-century perfumery. Modern perfumers also frequently use benzyl salicylate to expand white floral accords (gardenia, jasmine, lily), create a warm "sun-kissed" solar effect, soften marine fragrances, and increase the realism of orchid, tropical floral, and sunscreen-inspired compositions.
Benz Sal.avoid_notes_full:
Benzyl salicylate rarely "clashes" chemically with other perfume materials, but professionals avoid allowing it to dominate compositions because excessive amounts tend to flatten, blur, or mute brighter notes. Since its odor is intentionally diffuse, overdosing can reduce contrast within a fragrance, causing sparkling citrus, crisp green materials, or transparent aquatic accords to lose their freshness. Experienced perfumers therefore treat it as a structural ingredient rather than a featured note: enough to support the composition, but not so much that every floral accord acquires the same heavy salicylic "sunscreen" character. Community discussions among trained perfumers likewise caution that while benzyl salicylate is an excellent blender, excessive use can dull a composition if the surrounding accord is not well balanced.

From a semantic standpoint, benzyl salicylate is also generally avoided in fragrances that depend on sharp realism rather than smooth elegance. For example, if the goal is to recreate freshly squeezed orange, raw eucalyptus, crisp pine needles, fresh-cut grass, vinegar, or harsh industrial odors, large amounts of benzyl salicylate tend to make these materials feel overly creamy, floral, or cosmetic. Likewise, highly smoky accords dominated by birch tar or intensely animalic accords dominated by isovaleric acid can become oddly polished if too much benzyl salicylate is added. Experts instead reserve it for compositions where softness, elegance, and diffusion are desirable rather than raw authenticity.

Sandalwood.note: Woody, creamy, soft, warm, slightly sweet base note

avoid_with.name: Vanilla Sugar + Almond Extract
avoid_with.reason: sweet gourmand character competes with sandalwood's soft creamy-woody profile

avoid_with.name: Birch tar oil + Coffee + Clove Bud
avoid_with.reason: both compete for the woody backbone instead of complementing

Sandalwood.mixing_notes_full:
Sandalwood is one of perfumery's most important foundation materials, valued for its exceptionally smooth, creamy, woody warmth and remarkable ability to unify otherwise contrasting notes. Unlike drier woods such as cedar or cypress, sandalwood possesses a soft, milky quality that rounds sharp edges without noticeably changing the identity of the fragrance. Professional perfumers frequently use sandalwood both as a recognizable note and as a structural fixative, extending longevity while giving floral, citrus, spicy, and resinous accords a luxurious, velvety texture. Because its odor is relatively stable throughout evaporation, sandalwood often forms the backbone of oriental, woody, amber, floral, and modern minimalist fragrances.

Professionally, sandalwood is most commonly paired with rose, jasmine, lavender, vanilla, benzoin, patchouli, cedarwood, frankincense, myrrh, citrus oils, cardamom, black pepper, and soft musks. Citrus notes brighten sandalwood's creamy richness, while florals gain depth and elegance without becoming heavy. Vanilla and benzoin reinforce its comforting warmth, whereas spices such as cardamom or black pepper introduce contrast that prevents sandalwood from feeling overly smooth. Many classic woody fragrances rely on sandalwood as the central bridge connecting bright openings with rich, long-lasting base notes.
Sandalwood.avoid_notes_full:
Although sandalwood is highly versatile, professionals generally avoid overdosing it in fragrances intended to communicate sharp freshness or strong realism. Large amounts can blur crisp citrus, fresh-cut herbs, green leaves, marine accords, and highly transparent florals by coating them with a creamy, woody softness. Likewise, fragrances intended to smell icy, metallic, or highly volatile often lose their intended clarity when sandalwood becomes dominant.

Sandalwood also requires restraint when paired with extremely smoky or intensely animalic materials. Heavy birch tar, excessive isovaleric acid, or large amounts of harsh acidic materials may compete with sandalwood's refined warmth rather than benefiting from it. In these situations, perfumers typically allow sandalwood to remain a supporting structural note while limiting its concentration so that it provides smoothness without masking the distinctive character of the primary accord.

Clove Bud + Cumin.mixing_notes_full: This is an equal-parts spice blend of clove bud and cumin rather than clove alone. Clove still supplies its classic warm, pungent, slightly medicinal-sweet spiciness. Cumin adds an earthy, dry, slightly bitter and savory-adjacent facet that clove alone doesn't have, giving the blend more range across both sweet-spice contexts (chai, cinnamon roll, mulled drinks -- where clove's warmth still leads) and savory-spice contexts (curries, roasted/grilled food, garlic-adjacent savory targets -- where cumin's earthiness becomes more useful than clove alone could offer).
Clove Bud + Cumin.avoid_notes_full: Same core caution as clove alone: avoid high levels in fragrances that depend on clean transparency (delicate florals, aquatic accords, minimalist musks), where the combined spice signature will dominate. Cumin's earthy, slightly sweaty-savory facet also means this blend should be used more cautiously than clove alone in delicate floral or fresh-citrus targets, where cumin's dry earthiness reads as an unwanted savory intrusion rather than warmth.

Lavender + Rose.mixing_notes_full:
This is an equal-parts floral bouquet of lavender and rose rather than a single-note floral. Lavender contributes calming, herbaceous, aromatic-fresh facets and enough green freshness to bridge citrus and woody materials. Rose contributes a dewy, rosy, slightly honeyed petal-sweetness that softens lavender's herbal edge and gives the blend more body than lavender alone -- useful whenever a target calls for floral richness and depth rather than lavender's cleaner, more austere character alone.

Professionally this bouquet pairs well with the same partners lavender favored individually -- citrus (Orange), warm gourmand bases (Vanilla Sugar + Almond Extract), and soft woods (Sandalwood) -- while the added rose gives it more room to carry floral-forward targets (rose, floral perfumes) on its own without needing a supporting citrus or woody note.
Lavender + Rose.avoid_notes_full: The same materials that clashed with lavender alone -- isovaleric acid, vinegar, birch tar/coffee/clove, and heavy eucalyptus -- still overwhelm or distort this blend, and now do so across two floral facets at once rather than one, so the antiseptic/medicinal drift happens even faster and is harder to correct for. The added rose also makes the blend noticeably richer and more assertive than lavender alone, so it can read as "too much perfume" or "too sweet/soapy" for targets that want a clean, transparent, or sharp-fresh character (chemical/solvent targets, crisp citrus-soda freshness) -- in those cases keep this blend to a smaller share of the composition rather than letting it dominate.

Orange.mixing_notes_full:
Orange essential oil is one of perfumery's classic citrus top notes, prized for its bright, juicy, sweet freshness and immediate recognizability. Compared with lemon, orange is softer, rounder, and more naturally sweet, allowing it to bridge fresh citrus openings with floral, gourmand, herbal, and woody compositions. Because of its high volatility, orange primarily contributes the opening impression of a fragrance, creating an uplifting effect before gradually revealing the underlying heart and base notes. Professional perfumers frequently use orange to introduce warmth and approachability without the sharp acidity associated with other citrus materials.

Orange pairs exceptionally well with lavender, rosemary, eucalyptus, jasmine, neroli, sandalwood, cedarwood, vanilla, benzoin, cinnamon, clove, cardamom, ginger, and soft musks. Vanilla transforms orange into comforting gourmand accords reminiscent of baked desserts, while spices create familiar seasonal combinations such as mulled citrus or spiced orange. Woody materials provide structure and longevity, whereas aromatic herbs preserve freshness. These combinations make orange one of the most versatile citrus ingredients across fine fragrance, personal care, and household products.
Orange.avoid_notes_full:
Orange performs poorly when combined in large quantities with materials that immediately dominate perception. Highly smoky ingredients such as birch tar, strongly sulfurous animalic materials such as isovaleric acid, or concentrated acidic notes can quickly overwhelm orange's delicate top-note character, causing the fragrance to lose its fresh identity before the opening develops. Rather than enhancing realism, these combinations often suggest spoiled fruit, burnt citrus peel, or industrial cleaning products.

Professional perfumers therefore typically support orange with bridging materials instead of pairing it directly with multiple aggressive odorants. When smoky or fermented effects are desired, orange is usually present only in trace quantities to introduce brightness before disappearing naturally. Its greatest strength lies in providing freshness, optimism, and recognizability rather than competing against dark or highly persistent materials.

Vanilla Sugar + Almond Extract.mixing_notes_full:
This is an equal-parts gourmand blend of vanilla sugar and almond extract rather than vanilla alone. Vanilla sugar contributes the familiar warm, creamy, caramelized-sweet backbone; almond extract adds a nutty, marzipan-like, slightly bitter-sweet facet (comparable to benzaldehyde/amaretto notes) that gives the blend more bakery/confectionery depth than vanilla alone -- useful for targets like baked goods, pastries, and cookie-adjacent gourmand smells where plain vanilla read as one-dimensional.

It keeps all of plain vanilla's traditional strengths as a softening, harmonizing base note -- smoothing sharp citrus, taming spice, enriching woods -- while the almond facet gives it an edge that's especially useful for cinnamon-roll, cake, and pastry-type targets that want a "baked" character rather than a purely creamy-sweet one.
Vanilla Sugar + Almond Extract.avoid_notes_full: Same cautions as vanilla alone: avoid letting it dominate crisp, dry, or mineral-fresh targets (oceanic, citrus, green, herbal-cooling), where it will read as overly sweet/confectionery. The added almond-extract facet makes this blend read even more distinctly "bakery/dessert" than vanilla alone, so it should be used sparingly (or not at all) in savory, smoky, meaty, or woody/resinous compositions -- feedback data consistently shows this ingredient reading as unwanted sweetness whenever it's added to savory, smoky, or woody targets, and the added almond note makes that clash even more noticeable.

Birch tar oil + Coffee + Clove Bud.mixing_notes_full: This is an equal-parts smoky/roasted blend of birch tar, coffee, and clove rather than birch tar alone. Birch tar still supplies the core smoky, tarry, leathery, burnt-phenolic character. Coffee adds a dark, bitter, roasted depth that reinforces the "charred/roasted" read without adding sweetness, and clove contributes warm, pungent spice that bridges the smoke into food-adjacent contexts (BBQ, roasted meat, mulled/spiced accords) more naturally than birch tar alone. Feedback data shows this combination working especially well as the dominant note for grilled/BBQ/roasted-meat and coffee-forward targets, where it should typically lead the composition (40%+ of the blend) rather than sit as a minor accent.
Birch tar oil + Coffee + Clove Bud.avoid_notes_full: Same core caution as birch tar alone: avoid dominant use in fragrances built around freshness, cleanliness, or delicate transparency, since even a small overdose reads as dirty, burnt, or medicinal. The added coffee and clove facets make this blend read as more "food-roasted" than pure birch tar, so it pairs poorly with anything meant to read as fresh, green, or floral, and -- per participant feedback -- adding Vanilla Sugar + Almond Extract into a composition already led by this blend tends to read as unwanted sweetness rather than a complementary "toasted dessert" note; keep sweet gourmand materials to a light trace, if used at all, when this blend is dominant.

Eucalyptus.mixing_notes_full:
Eucalyptus is widely used in perfumery and aromatherapy for its cool, camphoraceous, fresh herbal character. Unlike peppermint, which emphasizes minty sweetness, eucalyptus contributes a cleaner, greener, and more medicinal freshness that immediately evokes forests, spas, and respiratory clarity. Because of its high volatility, eucalyptus functions primarily as a top note, providing an immediate cooling sensation before transitioning into supporting herbal and woody accords. Professional perfumers frequently use eucalyptus to brighten otherwise dense fragrances while introducing a sense of cleanliness and vitality.

Common professional pairings include orange, lemon, bergamot, lavender, rosemary, pine, cedarwood, sandalwood, tea tree, sage, thyme, and soft woods. Citrus oils soften eucalyptus's medicinal sharpness, while lavender creates the classic relaxing spa accord found in many wellness products. Woody materials stabilize its freshness and prevent it from disappearing too quickly. Small quantities are also used to enhance forest, herbal, and green botanical accords by contributing realistic aromatic complexity.
Eucalyptus.avoid_notes_full:
Because eucalyptus possesses a strong camphoraceous character, professionals avoid allowing it to dominate fragrances centered on delicate florals, creamy gourmands, or rich oriental compositions. Excessive eucalyptus can transform elegant floral bouquets into medicinal products or suppress the comforting warmth of vanilla and other sweet materials. Similarly, highly powdery fragrances may lose their softness if eucalyptus becomes the primary top note.

Eucalyptus also combines poorly with multiple harsh realism materials at the same time. Strong birch tar, concentrated vinegar, or excessive isovaleric acid often reinforce medicinal, antiseptic, or industrial associations instead of increasing realism. When these materials must coexist, experienced perfumers introduce intermediate bridge notes such as woods, citrus, or soft florals so that eucalyptus contributes freshness without becoming the dominant perceptual feature.

Cognac.mixing_notes_full:
"Cognac" in perfumery is not intended to smell exactly like the beverage itself, but rather to evoke its boozy warmth, oak maturation, dried fruits, caramelized sugars, and alcoholic lift. It functions as a transitional note between bright volatile top notes and deep gourmand or woody bases. Professional perfumers use cognac accords to create an impression of maturity, richness, and luxury without allowing the fragrance to smell simply alcoholic. In many modern niche perfumes, the cognac accord disappears quickly after application, leaving behind woods, tobacco, amber, vanilla, and spices that collectively recreate the lingering memory of an aged spirit.

The materials most frequently paired with cognac include vanilla, benzoin, tonka bean, oak, cedarwood, sandalwood, patchouli, tobacco, leather, coffee, cocoa, dried fruits, cinnamon, clove, labdanum, and amber. Vanilla and tonka soften the alcohol, while woods recreate barrel aging. Tobacco and leather contribute sophistication, and coffee or cocoa reinforce roasted nuances. Rather than existing independently, cognac almost always serves as a bridge that makes gourmand, woody, or oriental fragrances feel richer and more realistic. Many contemporary niche fragrances built around whiskey, rum, bourbon, or cognac rely on this same structural strategy.
Cognac.avoid_notes_full:
Cognac accords generally conflict with fragrance themes centered on crystalline freshness. Delicate citrus colognes, marine aquatics, icy mint fragrances, or transparent green florals depend on lightness and evaporation, whereas cognac introduces warmth, sweetness, and density. Combining these contrasting themes without an intentional artistic concept often produces a confusing fragrance that lacks a coherent identity. For this reason, perfumers rarely combine strong cognac accords directly with large amounts of eucalyptus, ozonic materials, or minimalist aquatic compositions.

Similarly, cognac requires restraint around strong acidic and sulfurous materials. Excessive vinegar or highly animalic ingredients such as isovaleric acid can easily transform the intended impression of refined aged spirits into one resembling spoiled alcohol or industrial solvent. When fermentation notes are desired—as in wine, whiskey, or dark fruit accords—professionals generally rely on trace acidic nuances supported by vanilla, dried fruits, woods, and spices rather than allowing sourness to dominate. The resulting composition communicates sophistication rather than harshness, preserving the luxurious identity expected of a cognac accord.

Vinegar.mixing_notes_full:
Unlike vanilla or lavender, vinegar is rarely used as a character note. Instead, perfumers use extremely small amounts of acetic acid to introduce realism into fermented, alcoholic, fruity, and gourmand accords. The goal is almost never to make the fragrance smell like household vinegar. Rather, trace acidity creates the same perceptual effect that acidity creates in food: it cuts sweetness, increases contrast, and makes surrounding ingredients appear more vivid. PerfumersWorld specifically recommends acetic acid only in high dilution and lists applications in woody blends, butter, butterscotch, cheese, chocolate, grape, raspberry, rum, strawberry, wine, pickles, and spice accords.

Historically, vinegar even has a long history in perfumery through toilet vinegars (vinaigres de toilette). Nineteenth-century perfumers macerated herbs such as lavender, rosemary, eucalyptus, sage, cloves, and citrus blossoms in wine vinegar or acetic acid to produce aromatic vinegars that served both hygienic and fragrant purposes. Modern niche perfumery occasionally revives this tradition. For example, Diptyque's Vinaigre de Toilette opens with a recognizable vinegar impression before transitioning into neroli, herbs, incense, pepper, woods, and resin, demonstrating that vinegar functions best as a brief structural accent rather than a persistent odor.
Vinegar.avoid_notes_full:
Professional perfumers generally avoid combining vinegar with fragrance themes whose defining quality is purity, softness, or creamy elegance. White florals such as jasmine, tuberose, gardenia, lily-of-the-valley, and powdery violet rely on smooth diffusion and rounded transitions. Even small overdoses of acetic acid can abruptly introduce a sour edge that makes these flowers appear wilted or fermented rather than fresh. Likewise, excessive acidity can spoil delicate citrus accords by changing the perception from "freshly peeled orange" to "old orange juice" or "spoiled fruit." Consequently, perfumers using vinegar almost always counterbalance it with floral, woody, or balsamic materials before allowing it to become perceptible.

Vinegar also competes poorly with other harsh high-impact materials. Pairing concentrated acetic acid with birch tar, isovaleric acid, or excessive eucalyptus frequently produces medicinal, industrial, or cleaning-product associations because all four materials are extremely salient to the human olfactory system. Rather than reinforcing realism, they compete for perceptual dominance. Expert perfumers therefore generally allow only one "harsh" material to dominate, while the others remain in trace amounts and are buffered by bridge materials such as vanilla, woods, spices, amber, or soft florals.

Isovaleric acid.mixing_notes_full:
Isovaleric acid is one of perfumery's classic trace realism materials. In isolation it is immediately recognizable as sweaty feet, aged cheese, dirty socks, or body odor. However, at concentrations hundreds or even thousands of times lower than its detection threshold in isolation, it becomes extraordinarily valuable because it introduces the subtle biological imperfections found in real foods, natural materials, and living organisms. Professional perfumers almost never intend for consumers to identify isovaleric acid directly. Instead, they use minute quantities to make cheese, butter, yogurt, fermented dairy, chocolate, roasted coffee, leather, tobacco, certain fruits, and animalic accords feel significantly more authentic. Experienced perfumers working with isovaleric acid routinely discuss using concentrations in the parts-per-million or even parts-per-billion range because of its exceptional odor power.

Professionally, isovaleric acid is most often supported by vanilla, butter, milk accords, lactones, coffee, cocoa, tobacco, leather, woods, amber, and light fruity esters. These ingredients provide context that transforms its unpleasant standalone odor into a convincing component of a larger accord. For example, chocolate without trace acidic or animalic nuances often smells flat or artificial, whereas the addition of minute amounts of isovaleric acid can produce a more realistic roasted depth. Similarly, aged cheese accords depend on balancing isovaleric acid with buttery, creamy, and lactic materials rather than allowing the acid to dominate. In expert hands, isovaleric acid is therefore not a "bad smell" but a realism enhancer that adds biological complexity unavailable through pleasant materials alone.
Isovaleric acid.avoid_notes_full:
The most common mistake when using isovaleric acid is pairing it with fragrances whose identity depends on cleanliness or freshness. Citrus colognes, oceanic aquatics, transparent musks, fresh laundry accords, airy florals, and herbal spa fragrances communicate hygiene. Even trace overdoses of isovaleric acid immediately disrupt this perception because humans are evolutionarily extremely sensitive to body-odor molecules. Instead of increasing realism, the fragrance begins to smell contaminated. Professional perfumers therefore almost never use isovaleric acid in compositions intended to communicate cleanliness unless the amount is so low that it is effectively undetectable.

Isovaleric acid also interacts poorly with other dominant unpleasant materials when no supporting framework exists. Large amounts of vinegar increase sourness, birch tar adds burnt phenolics, and eucalyptus emphasizes medicinal cooling. Together these materials create additive harshness rather than complexity. Experts instead rely on the principle of single-feature dominance: if isovaleric acid provides the biological realism, smoky or acidic materials are reduced to trace levels, and warm bridge notes such as vanilla, woods, tobacco, chocolate, amber, or spices are introduced to integrate the accord. This principle explains why real cheese, coffee, leather, and tobacco fragrances remain pleasant despite containing molecules that are individually offensive.

avoid_with.name: Isovaleric acid

Thyme + Olive Leaf + Seaweed + Garlic.mixing_notes_full: This is an equal-parts savoury blend of thyme, olive leaf, seaweed, and garlic rather than seaweed alone. Seaweed still supplies the salty, iodine-rich marine-umami backbone. Thyme adds an earthy, herbal, slightly medicinal-green facet; olive leaf contributes a bitter-green, slightly tannic quality; and garlic adds sharp, pungent, sulfurous realism. Together the four give this odorant far more range across savoury/umami targets than seaweed alone -- particularly pungent allium/vegetable targets (garlic, savoury sauces) and herb-forward savoury food, where the added thyme and garlic facets are the key drivers rather than seaweed's marine character.
Thyme + Olive Leaf + Seaweed + Garlic.avoid_notes_full: Because this blend is now both marine AND pungently savoury/herbal at once, it should be used even more cautiously than seaweed alone around sweet, clean, or delicate targets -- feedback data shows seaweed alone already overdosing badly in dessert and fresh-vegetable contexts, and the added garlic and thyme facets make that clash more pronounced, not less. Avoid pairing at high levels with Vanilla Sugar + Almond Extract or other sweet gourmand materials, and use restraint around fresh, watery, or green-vegetal targets (e.g. cucumber) where the salty-pungent character reads as wrong rather than complementary.
